Business systems

Before you buy another AI tool, let’s find the work that is wearing you out.

If your customers, payments and follow-ups live in different conversations, start with a clearer process.

Anzolo Kpazhi Hope15 November 2026 · 2 min read

You have answered messages all day, but by evening you still cannot say which customer is waiting, which order is ready or who promised to follow up. You are busy. Your team is busy. Yet the work feels as though it is slipping through your hands.

If that sounds familiar, I want you to pause before buying another tool. Let us first understand where the work loses its shape. The solution I would help you build starts with a visible process, then adds automation where it earns its place.

Choose one uncomfortable moment

Picture a small retailer taking orders through WhatsApp. A customer asks for a price, another sends a payment screenshot and a supplier changes a delivery date. This is an illustrative situation, but you may recognise the pressure. The phone holds the conversation; it does not automatically hold a reliable record of the business.

Write down the moment that causes the most repeated confusion. It might be an unanswered enquiry, an order handed to the wrong person or a quotation nobody follows up. Choose one. A useful starting point is small enough for you to explain without opening a presentation.

Give every enquiry a home

For that one process, record the customer, request, current status, responsible person and next action. Add a due date to the next action. You can begin in an existing spreadsheet if it meets your access and privacy needs. The point is that your team can find the same information.

Keep the statuses understandable: new, awaiting clarification, awaiting payment verification, ready and completed. A payment screenshot should not silently turn an order into a verified payment. Give that decision to the person and source your business actually trusts.

Now decide where AI helps

An assistant could draft a response, summarise a long conversation or propose fields for the order. Your application should check the catalogue, price, stock and permissions. The person approving a consequential action should see what will happen before it happens.

This is the direction of my work through ECHUKU, including my focus on business systems and the KONTA ERP/POS project: help people see and manage their operations. That statement describes my product direction; it is not a claim that every proposed capability has already been validated in every setting.

Run a one-week experiment

Record how long the chosen task takes and how often someone needs to correct or chase it. Introduce the clearer process for a comparable workload. Then compare the results. If things improve, find out why. If they do not, inspect the process before adding another layer of software.

You do not need to transform the whole business this week. You need one problem that is visible, one person responsible for it and one improvement you can explain. That is where I would begin with you.

Your next step

Pick ten recent enquiries. Can you identify an owner and a next action for every one?
